829: -doc false.
830: -spec handle_call(term(), gen_server:from(), state()) -> {reply | noreply, term(), state()}.
831: handle_call({set_pattern, M, F, A}, _From, #tprof_state{trace_map = Map, type = Type} = State) ->
832:     {Reply, NewMap} = enable_pattern(M, F, A, Map, Type),
833:     {reply, Reply, State#tprof_state{trace_map = NewMap}};
834: handle_call({clear_pattern, M, F, A}, _From, #tprof_state{trace_map = Map, type = Type} = State) ->
835:     {Ret, NewMap} = disable_pattern(M, F, A, Map, Type),
836:     {reply, Ret, State#tprof_state{trace_map = NewMap}};
837: handle_call(get_trace_map, _From, #tprof_state{trace_map = Map} = State) ->
838:     {reply, Map, State};
839: handle_call(pause, _From, #tprof_state{paused = true} = State) ->
840:     {reply, not_running, State};
841: handle_call(pause, _From, #tprof_state{trace_map = Map, paused = false, type = Type} = State) ->
842:     foreach(Map, pause, Type),
843:     {reply, ok, State#tprof_state{paused = true}};
844: handle_call(continue, _From, #tprof_state{paused = false} = State) ->
845:     {reply, running, State};
846: handle_call(continue, _From, #tprof_state{trace_map = Map, type = Type} = State) ->
847:     foreach(Map, true, Type),
848:     {reply, ok, State#tprof_state{paused = false}};
849: handle_call(restart, _From, #tprof_state{trace_map = Map, type = Type} = State) ->
850:     foreach(Map, restart, Type),
851:     {reply, ok, State#tprof_state{paused = false}};
852: handle_call(collect, _From, #tprof_state{trace_map = Map, type = Type} = State) ->
853:     {reply, collect(Map, Type), State};
854: handle_call({profile, What, Options}, From, #tprof_state{ad_hoc = undefined, trace_map = Map, type = Type} = State) ->
855:     %% ad-hoc profile routed via gen_server to handle 'EXIT' signal
856:     {Pid, Timer, Patterns, RootSet, NewMap} = ad_hoc_run(What, Options, Map, Type),
857:     {noreply, State#tprof_state{ad_hoc = {Pid, Timer, Patterns, RootSet, From}, trace_map = NewMap}};
858: handle_call({profile, _What, _Options}, _From, State) ->
859:     {reply, {error, running}, State}.

861: -doc false.

866: -doc false.
867: -spec handle_info(term(), state()) -> {noreply, state()}.
868: handle_info({'EXIT', Pid, Reason}, #tprof_state{ad_hoc = {Pid, Timer, Patterns, RootSet, From},
869:     trace_map = Map, type = Type} = State) ->
870:     _ = disable_trace(RootSet),
871:     Profile = collect(Map, Type),

878:     _ = disable_trace(RootSet),
879:     Profile = collect(Map, Type),

892: -include_lib("kernel/include/logger.hrl").

894: %% Add the trace of the specified module to the accumulator
895: collect_trace(Mod, FunList, Acc, Type) ->
896:     {Fail, Ret} = lists:foldl(
897:         fun ({Fun, Arity}, {Fail, Prev}) ->
898:             case combine_trace(erlang:trace_info({Mod, Fun, Arity}, Type)) of
899:                 skip ->
900:                     {Fail, Prev};
901:                 fail ->
902:                     {true, Prev};
903:                 Tr ->
904:                     {Fail, [{Mod, Fun, Arity, Tr} | Prev]}
905:             end
906:         end, {false, Acc}, FunList),
907:     %% module may have been hot-code reloaded, or tracing was broken by something else
908:     Fail andalso begin
909:         ?LOG_WARNING(
910:             "tprof encountered an error tracing module ~s, was it reloaded or untraced?",
911:             [Mod])
912:         end,
913:     Ret.
914: 
915: %% It is possible that due to hot code reload event
916: %% some function is no longer traced, while it was supposed to.
917: %% Reinstating tracing automatically is wrong thing to do, because
918: %% statistics won't be correct anyway. Hence the warning in the user
919: %% guide, guarding against hot code reload while tracing.
920: combine_trace({_, false}) -> fail;
921: combine_trace({call_count, 0}) -> skip;
922: combine_trace({call_count, Num}) -> [{all, Num, Num}];
923: combine_trace({call_time, Times}) ->
924:     case [{Pid, Calls, S * 1000000 + Us} || {Pid, Calls, S, Us} <- Times] of
925:         [] ->
926:             skip;
927:         NonZero ->
928:             NonZero
929:     end;
930: combine_trace({call_memory, Mem}) ->
931:     case [{Pid, Calls, Words} || {Pid, Calls, Words} <- Mem, Words > 0] of
932:         [] ->
933:             skip;
934:         NonZero ->
935:             NonZero
936:     end.
937: 
938: %% Inspection: iterate over collected traces, return map of
939: %%  #{Pid => [{M, {F, A}, Calls, Measurement, PerCall, Percentage}], unsorted.
940: inspect_processes([], Acc) ->
941:     maps:map(
942:         fun (_Pid, {Total, Lines}) ->
943:             {Total, [{M, {F, A}, Calls, Measurement, PerCall, divide(Measurement * 100, Total)}
944:                 || {M, F, A, Calls, Measurement, PerCall} <- Lines]}
945:         end, Acc);
946: inspect_processes([{_M, _F, _A, []} | Tail], Acc) ->
947:     inspect_processes(Tail, Acc);
948: inspect_processes([{M, F, A, [{Pid, Calls, Mem} | TripletTail]} | Tail], Acc) ->
949:     ProfLine = {M, F, A, Calls, Mem, divide(Mem, Calls)},
950:     inspect_processes([{M, F, A, TripletTail} | Tail],
951:         maps:update_with(Pid, fun ({Grand, L}) -> {Grand + Mem, [ProfLine | L]} end, {Mem, [ProfLine]}, Acc)).
952: 
953: %% Inspection: remove Pid information from the Profile, return list of
954: %%  [{M, F, A, TotalCalls, Measurement, PerCall, Percentage}]
955: inspect_total(M, F, A, GrandTotal, Mems) ->
956:     {TC, TM} = lists:foldl(
957:         fun ({_Pid, Calls, Mem}, {TotalCalls, TotalMem}) ->
958:             {TotalCalls + Calls, TotalMem + Mem}
959:         end, {0, 0}, Mems),
960:     {M, {F, A}, TC, TM, divide(TM, TC), divide(TM * 100, GrandTotal)}.
961: 
962: divide(_,0) -> 0.0;
963: divide(T,N) -> T/N.
964: 
965: %% Returns "sort by" column index
966: column(module) -> {1, ascending};
967: column(function) -> {2, ascending};
968: column(calls) -> {3, ascending};
969: column(measurement) -> {4, ascending};
970: column(measurement_per_call) -> {5, ascending};
971: column(percent) -> {6, ascending}.
972: 
973: %% Sorts by column name, ascending/descending
974: inspect_sort(Profile, undefined) ->
975:     Profile;
976: inspect_sort(Profile, {Column, ascending}) when is_integer(Column) ->
977:     lists:keysort(Column, Profile);
978: inspect_sort(Profile, {Column, descending}) when is_integer(Column) ->
979:     lists:reverse(lists:keysort(Column, Profile));
980: inspect_sort(Profile, {Column, Direction}) when is_atom(Column) ->
981:     {Col, _Skip} = column(Column),
982:     inspect_sort(Profile, {Col, Direction});
983: inspect_sort(Profile, Column) when is_atom(Column) ->
984:     inspect_sort(Profile, column(Column)).

986: %% Formats the inspected profile to the Device, which could be [] meaning
987: %%  default output.
988: format_impl(Device, Empty) when Empty =:= #{} ->
989:     format_out(Device, "Trace is empty~n", []);
990: format_impl(Device, #{all := {Type, Total, Inspected}}) ->
991:     format_each(Device, Type, Total, Inspected);
992: format_impl(Device, Inspected) when is_map(Inspected) ->
993:     %% grab the total-total words
994:     GrandTotal = maps:fold(fun (_Pid, {_Type, Total, _Profile}, Acc) -> Acc + Total end, 0, Inspected),
995:     %% per-process printout
996:     maps:foreach(
997:         fun(Pid, {Type, Total, Each}) ->
998:             format_out(Device, "~n****** Process ~w  --  ~.2f% of total *** ~n",
999:                 [Pid, divide(100 * Total, GrandTotal)]),
1000:             format_each(Device, Type, Total, Each)
1001:         end, Inspected).
1002: 
1003: format_each(Device, call_count, _Total, Inspected) ->
1004:     %% viewport size
1005:     %% Viewport = case io:columns() of {ok, C} -> C; _ -> 80 end,
1006:     %% layout: module and fun/arity columns are resizable, the rest are not
1007:     %% convert all lines to strings
1008:     {Widths, Lines} = lists:foldl(
1009:         fun ({Mod, {F, A}, Calls, _Value, _VPC, Percent}, {Widths, Ln}) ->
1010:             Line = [lists:flatten(io_lib:format("~tw:~tw/~w", [Mod, F, A])),
1011:                 integer_to_list(Calls), float_to_list(Percent, [{decimals, 2}])],
1012:             NewWidths = [erlang:max(Old, New) || {Old, New} <- lists:zip([string:length(L) || L <- Line], Widths)],
1013:             {NewWidths, [Line | Ln]}
1014:         end, {[0, 5, 5], []}, Inspected),
1015:     %% figure our max column widths according to viewport (cut off module/funArity)
1016:     FilteredWidths = Widths,
1017:     %% figure out formatting line
1018:     Fmt = lists:flatten(io_lib:format("~~.~wts  ~~~ws  [~~~ws]~~n", FilteredWidths)),
1019:     %% print using this format
1020:     format_out(Device, Fmt, ["FUNCTION", "CALLS", "%"]),
1021:     [format_out(Device, Fmt, Line) || Line <- lists:reverse(Lines)],
1022:     format_out(Device, Fmt, [" ", " ", "100.0"]);
1023: format_each(Device, call_time, Total, Inspected) ->
1024:     format_labelled(Device, "TIME (μs)", Total, Inspected);
1025: format_each(Device, call_memory, Total, Inspected) ->
1026:     format_labelled(Device, "WORDS", Total, Inspected).
1027: 
1028: format_labelled(Device, Label, Total, Inspected) ->
1029:     %% viewport size
1030:     %% Viewport = case io:columns() of {ok, C} -> C; _ -> 80 end,
1031:     %% layout: module and fun/arity columns are resizable, the rest are not
1032:     %% convert all lines to strings
1033:     {Widths, Lines} = lists:foldl(
1034:         fun ({Mod, {F, A}, Calls, Value, VPC, Percent}, {Widths, Ln}) ->
1035:             Line = [lists:flatten(io_lib:format("~tw:~tw/~w", [Mod, F, A])),
1036:                 integer_to_list(Calls), integer_to_list(Value),
1037:                 float_to_list(VPC, [{decimals, 2}]),
1038:                 float_to_list(Percent, [{decimals, 2}])],
1039:             NewWidths = [erlang:max(Old, New) || {Old, New} <- lists:zip([string:length(L) || L <- Line], Widths)],
1040:             {NewWidths, [Line | Ln]}
1041:         end, {[0, 5, length(Label), 8, 5], []}, Inspected),
1042:     %% figure our max column widths according to viewport (cut off module/funArity)
1043:     FilteredWidths = Widths,
1044:     %% figure out formatting line
1045:     Fmt = lists:flatten(io_lib:format("~~.~wts  ~~~ws  ~~~wts  ~~~ws  [~~~ws]~~n", FilteredWidths)),
1046:     %% print using this format
1047:     format_out(Device, Fmt, ["FUNCTION", "CALLS", Label, "PER CALL", "%"]),
1048:     [format_out(Device, Fmt, Line) || Line <- lists:reverse(Lines)],
1049:     format_out(Device, Fmt, [" ", " ", integer_to_list(Total), " ", "100.0"]).
1050: 
1051: %% format implementation that uses [] as a way to tell "default output"
1052: format_out([], Fmt, Args) ->
1053:     io:format(Fmt, Args);
1054: format_out(Device, Fmt, Args) ->
1055:     io:format(Device, Fmt, Args).

1057: %% pattern collapse code
1058: enable_pattern('_', '_', '_', _Acc, Type) ->
1059:     %% need to re-trace everything, probably some new modules were loaded
1060:     %% discard any existing trace pattern
1061:     lists:foldl(
1062:         fun({Mod, _}, {Total, Acc}) ->
1063:             Plus = erlang:trace_pattern({Mod, '_', '_'}, true, [Type]),
1064:             {Total + Plus, Acc#{Mod => Mod:module_info(functions)}}
1065:         end, {0, #{}}, code:all_loaded());
1066: enable_pattern(Mod, '_', '_', Acc, Type) ->
1067:     %% code may have been hot-loaded, redo the trace
1068:     case erlang:trace_pattern({Mod, '_', '_'}, true, [Type]) of
1069:         0 ->
1070:             {{error, {trace_pattern, Mod, '_', '_'}}, Acc};
1071:         Traced ->
1072:             {Traced, Acc#{Mod => Mod:module_info(functions)}}
1073:     end;
1074: enable_pattern(Mod, Fun, '_', Acc, Type) ->
1075:     case erlang:trace_pattern({Mod, Fun, '_'}, true, [Type]) of
1076:         0 ->
1077:             {{error, {trace_pattern, Mod, Fun, '_'}}, Acc};
1078:         Traced ->
1079:             Added = [{F, A} || {F, A} <- Mod:module_info(functions), F =:= Fun],
1080:             NewMap = maps:update_with(Mod,
1081:                 fun (FAs) ->
1082:                     Added ++ [{F, A} || {F, A} <- FAs, F =/= Fun]
1083:                 end, Added, Acc),
1084:             {Traced, NewMap}
1085:     end;
1086: enable_pattern(Mod, Fun, Arity, Acc, Type) ->
1087:     case erlang:trace_pattern({Mod, Fun, Arity}, true, [Type]) of
1088:         0 ->
1089:             {{error, {trace_pattern, Mod, Fun, Arity}}, Acc};
1090:         1 ->
1091:             {1, maps:update_with(Mod,
1092:                 fun (FAs) -> [{Fun, Arity} | FAs -- [{Fun, Arity}]] end, [{Fun, Arity}], Acc)}
1093:     end.
1094: 
1095: %% pattern collapse code for un-tracing
1096: disable_pattern('_', '_', '_', _Acc, Type) ->
1097:     Traced = erlang:trace_pattern({'_', '_', '_'}, false, [Type]),
1098:     {Traced, #{}};
1099: disable_pattern(Mod, '_', '_', Acc, Type) when is_map_key(Mod, Acc) ->
1100:     Traced = erlang:trace_pattern({Mod, '_', '_'}, false, [Type]),
1101:     {Traced, maps:remove(Mod, Acc)};
1102: disable_pattern(Mod, Fun, '_', Acc, Type) when is_map_key(Mod, Acc) ->
1103:     Traced = erlang:trace_pattern({Mod, Fun, '_'}, false, [Type]),
1104:     {Traced, maps:update_with(Mod,
1105:         fun (FAs) -> [{F, A} || {F, A} <- FAs, F =/= Fun] end, Acc)};
1106: disable_pattern(Mod, Fun, Arity, Acc, Type) when is_map_key(Mod, Acc) ->
1107:     Traced = erlang:trace_pattern({Mod, Fun, Arity}, false, [Type]),

20: # Profiling
21: 
22: ## Do Not Guess About Performance - Profile
23: 
24: Even experienced software developers often guess wrong about where the
25: performance bottlenecks are in their programs. Therefore, profile your program
26: to see where the performance bottlenecks are and concentrate on optimizing them.
27: 
28: Erlang/OTP contains several tools to help finding bottlenecks:
29: 
30: - `m:tprof` is a tracing profiler that can measure call count, call time, or
31:   heap allocations per function call.
32: - `m:fprof` provides the most detailed information about where the program time
33:   is spent, but it significantly slows down the program it profiles.
34: - `m:dbg` is the generic erlang tracing frontend. By using the `timestamp` or
35:   `cpu_timestamp` options it can be used to time how long function calls in a
36:   live system take.
37: - `m:lcnt` is used to find contention points in the Erlang Run-Time System's
38:   internal locking mechanisms. It is useful when looking for bottlenecks in
39:   interaction between process, port, ets tables and other entities that can be
40:   run in parallel.
41: 
42: The tools are further described in [Tools](profiling.md#profiling_tools).
43: 
44: There are also several open source tools outside of Erlang/OTP that can be used
45: to help profiling. Some of them are:
46: 
47: - [erlgrind](https://github.com/isacssouza/erlgrind) can be used to visualize
48:   fprof data in kcachegrind.
49: - [eflame](https://github.com/proger/eflame) is an alternative to fprof that
50:   displays the profiling output as a flamegraph.
51: - [recon](https://ferd.github.io/recon/index.html) is a collection of Erlang
52:   profiling and debugging tools. This tool comes with an accompanying E-book
53:   called [Erlang in Anger](https://www.erlang-in-anger.com/).
54: - [perf](https://perf.wiki.kernel.org/index.php/Main_Page) is a sampling
55:   profiler for Linux that provides functionality similar to `fprof` but with
56:   much lower overhead. Profiling Erlang code is possible when the emulator has
57:   been started with the `+JPperf true` emulator flag, and is only available when
58:   the JIT is enabled.
59: 
60:   For more details about how to run `perf` see the
61:   [perf support](`e:erts:beamasm.md#linux-perf-support`) section in the BeamAsm
62:   internal documentation.
63: 
64: ## Memory profiling
65: 
66: ```text
67: eheap_alloc: Cannot allocate 1234567890 bytes of memory (of type "heap").
68: ```
69: 
70: The above slogan is one of the more common reasons for Erlang to terminate. For
71: unknown reasons the Erlang Run-Time System failed to allocate memory to use.
72: When this happens a crash dump is generated that contains information about the
73: state of the system as it ran out of memory. Use the
74: [`crashdump_viewer`](`e:observer:cdv_cmd.md`) to get a view of the memory being
75: used. Look for processes with large heaps or many messages, large ets tables,
76: etc.
77: 
78: When looking at memory usage in a running system the most basic function to get
79: information from is [`erlang:memory()`](`erlang:memory/0`). It returns the
80: current memory usage of the system. `m:instrument` can be used to get a more
81: detailed breakdown of where memory is used.
82: 
83: Processes, ports and ets tables can then be inspected using their respective
84: info functions, i.e. [`erlang:process_info/2 `](`m:erlang#process_info_memory`),
85: [`erlang:port_info/2 `](`m:erlang#port_info_memory`)and `ets:info/1`.
86: 
87: Sometimes the system can enter a state where the reported memory from
88: `erlang:memory(total)` is very different from the memory reported by the OS.
89: This can be because of internal fragmentation within the Erlang Run-Time System.
90: Data about how memory is allocated can be retrieved using
91: [`erlang:system_info(allocator)`](`m:erlang#system_info_allocator`). The data
92: you get from that function is very raw and not very pleasant to read.
93: [recon_alloc](http://ferd.github.io/recon/recon_alloc.html) can be used to
94: extract useful information from system_info statistics counters.
95: 
96: ## Large Systems
97: 
98: For a large system, it can be interesting to run profiling on a simulated and
99: limited scenario to start with. But bottlenecks have a tendency to appear or
100: cause problems only when many things are going on at the same time, and when
101: many nodes are involved. Therefore, it is also desirable to run profiling in a
102: system test plant on a real target system.
103: 
104: For a large system, you do not want to run the profiling tools on the whole
105: system. Instead you want to concentrate on central processes and modules, which
106: account for a big part of the execution.
107: 
108: There are also some tools that can be used to get a view of the whole system
109: with more or less overhead.
110: 
111: - `m:observer` is a GUI tool that can connect to remote nodes and display a
112:   variety of information about the running system.
113: - `m:etop` is a command line tool that can connect to remote nodes and display
114:   information similar to what the UNIX tool top shows.
115: - `m:msacc` allows the user to get a view of what the Erlang Run-Time system is
116:   spending its time doing. Has a very low overhead, which makes it useful to run
117:   in heavily loaded systems to get some idea of where to start doing more
118:   granular profiling.
119: 
120: ## What to Look For
121: 
122: When analyzing the result file from the profiling activity, look for functions
123: that are called many times and have a long "own" execution time (time excluding
124: calls to other functions). Functions that are called a lot of times can also be
125: interesting, as even small things can add up to quite a bit if repeated often.
126: Also ask yourself what you can do to reduce this time. The following are
127: appropriate types of questions to ask yourself:
128: 
129: - Is it possible to reduce the number of times the function is called?
130: - Can any test be run less often if the order of tests is changed?
131: - Can any redundant tests be removed?
132: - Does any calculated expression give the same result each time?
133: - Are there other ways to do this that are equivalent and more efficient?
134: - Can another internal data representation be used to make things more
135:   efficient?
136: 
137: These questions are not always trivial to answer. Some benchmarks might be
138: needed to back up your theory and to avoid making things slower if your theory
139: is wrong. For details, see [Benchmarking](profiling.md#benchmark).
140: 
141: ## Tools
142: 
143: [](){: #profiling_tools }
144: 
145: ### fprof
146: 
147: `fprof` measures the execution time for each function, both own time, that is,
148: how much time a function has used for its own execution, and accumulated time,
149: that is, including called functions. The values are displayed per process. You
150: also get to know how many times each function has been called.
151: 
152: `fprof` is based on trace to file to minimize runtime performance impact. Using
153: `fprof` is just a matter of calling a few library functions, see the `m:fprof`
154: manual page in Tools.
155: 
156: ### eprof
157: 
158: `eprof` is based on the Erlang `trace_info` BIFs. `eprof` shows how much time
159: has been used by each process, and in which function calls this time has been
160: spent. Time is shown as a percentage of total time and absolute time. For more
161: information, see the `m:eprof` manual page in Tools.
162: 
163: ### cprof
164: 
165: `cprof` is something in between `fprof` and `cover` regarding features. It
166: counts how many times each function is called when the program is run, on a per
167: module basis. `cprof` has a low performance degradation effect (compared with
168: `fprof`) and does not need to recompile any modules to profile (compared with
169: `cover`). For more information, see the `m:cprof` manual page in Tools.
170: 
171: ### Tool Summary
172: 
173: | _Tool_  | _Results_                           | _Size of Result_ | _Effects on Program Execution Time_ | _Records Number of Calls_ | _Records Execution Time_ | _Records Called by_ | _Records Garbage Collection_ |
174: | ------- | ----------------------------------- | ---------------- | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------ | ------------------- | ---------------------------- |
175: | `fprof` | Per process to screen/file          | Large            | Significant slowdown                | Yes                       | Total and own            | Yes                 | Yes                          |
176: | `eprof` | Per process/function to screen/file | Medium           | Small slowdown                      | Yes                       | Only total               | No                  | No                           |
177: | `cprof` | Per module to caller                | Small            | Small slowdown                      | Yes                       | No                       | No                  | No                           |
178: 
179: _Table: Tool Summary_
180: 
181: ### dbg
182: 
183: `dbg` is a generic Erlang trace tool. By using the `timestamp` or
184: `cpu_timestamp` options it can be used as a precision instrument to profile how
185: long time a function call takes for a specific process. This can be very useful
186: when trying to understand where time is spent in a heavily loaded system as it
187: is possible to limit the scope of what is profiled to be very small. For more
188: information, see the `m:dbg` manual page in Runtime Tools.
189: 
190: ### lcnt
191: 
192: `lcnt` is used to profile interactions in between entities that run in parallel.
193: For example if you have a process that all other processes in the system needs
194: to interact with (maybe it has some global configuration), then `lcnt` can be
195: used to figure out if the interaction with that process is a problem.
196: 
197: In the Erlang Run-time System entities are only run in parallel when there are
198: multiple schedulers. Therefore `lcnt` will show more contention points (and thus
199: be more useful) on systems using many schedulers on many cores.
200: 
201: For more information, see the `m:lcnt` manual page in Tools.
202: 
203: [](){: #benchmark }
204: 
205: ## Benchmarking
206: 
207: The main purpose of benchmarking is to find out which implementation of a given
208: algorithm or function is the fastest. Benchmarking is far from an exact science.
209: Today's operating systems generally run background tasks that are difficult to
210: turn off. Caches and multiple CPU cores do not facilitate benchmarking. It would
211: be best to run UNIX computers in single-user mode when benchmarking, but that is
212: inconvenient to say the least for casual testing.
213: 
214: Benchmarks can measure wall-clock time or CPU time.
215: 
216: - `timer:tc/3` measures wall-clock time. The advantage with wall-clock time is
217:   that I/O, swapping, and other activities in the operating system kernel are
218:   included in the measurements. The disadvantage is that the measurements vary a
219:   lot. Usually it is best to run the benchmark several times and note the
220:   shortest time, which is to be the minimum time that is possible to achieve
221:   under the best of circumstances.
222: - [statistics/1](`erlang:statistics/1`) with argument `runtime` measures CPU
223:   time spent in the Erlang virtual machine. The advantage with CPU time is that
224:   the results are more consistent from run to run. The disadvantage is that the
225:   time spent in the operating system kernel (such as swapping and I/O) is not
226:   included. Therefore, measuring CPU time is misleading if any I/O (file or
227:   socket) is involved.
228: 
229: It is probably a good idea to do both wall-clock measurements and CPU time
230: measurements.
231: 
232: Some final advice:
233: 
234: - The granularity of both measurement types can be high. Therefore, ensure that
235:   each individual measurement lasts for at least several seconds.
236: - To make the test fair, each new test run is to run in its own, newly created
237:   Erlang process. Otherwise, if all tests run in the same process, the later
238:   tests start out with larger heap sizes and therefore probably do fewer garbage
239:   collections. Also consider restarting the Erlang emulator between each test.
240: - Do not assume that the fastest implementation of a given algorithm on computer
241:   architecture X is also the fastest on computer architecture Y.

20: # Upcoming Potential Incompatibilities
21: 
22: ## Introduction
23: 
24: This document lists planned upcoming potential incompatibilities in Erlang/OTP.
25: 
26: ## OTP 27
27: 
28: ### Fun creator pid will always be local init process
29: 
30: As of OTP 27, the functions [`erlang:fun_info/1,2`](`erlang:fun_info/1`) will
31: always say that the local `init` process created all funs, regardless of which
32: process or node the fun was originally created on.
33: 
34: In OTP 28, the `{pid,_}`element will be removed altogether.
35: 
36: [](){: #maybe_expr }
37: 
38: ### Feature maybe_expr will be enabled by default
39: 
40: As of OTP 27, the `maybe_expr` feature will be approved and enabled by default.
41: That means that code that uses the unquoted atom `maybe` will fail to compile.
42: All uses of `maybe` as an atom will need to be quoted. Alternatively, as a
43: short-term solution, the `maybe_expr` feature can be disabled.
44: 
45: It is recommend to quote all uses of the atom `maybe` as soon as possible. The
46: compiler option `warn_keywords` can be used to emit warnings about all
47: occurrences of `maybe` without quotes.
48: 
49: [](){: #new_re_engine }
50: 
51: ### The re module will use a different regular expression engine
52: 
53: The functionality of module `m:re` is currently provided by the PCRE library,
54: which is no longer actively maintained. Therefore, in OTP 27, we will switch to
55: a different regular expression library.
56: 
57: The source code for PCRE used by the `re` module has been modified by the OTP
58: team to ensure that a regular expression match would yield when matching huge
59: input binaries and/or when using demanding (back-tracking) regular expressions.
60: Because of the those modifications, moving to a new version of PCRE has always
61: been a time-consuming process because all of the modifications had to be applied
62: by hand again to the updated PCRE source code.
63: 
64: Most likely, the new regular expression library will be
65: [RE2](https://github.com/google/re2). RE2 guarantees that the match time is
66: linear in the length of input string, and it also eschews recursion to avoid
67: stack overflow. That should make it possible to use RE2 without modifying its
68: source code. For more information about why RE2 is a good choice, see
69: [WhyRE2](https://github.com/google/re2/wiki/WhyRE2).
70: 
71: Some of implications of this change are:
72: 
73: - We expect that the functions in the `re` module will continue to be supported,
74:   although some of the options are likely to be dis-continued.
75: - It is likely that only pattern matching of UTF8-encoded binaries will be
76:   supported (not Latin1-encoded binaries).
77: - In order to guarantee the linear-time performance, RE2 does not support all
78:   the constructs in regular expression patterns that PCRE do. For example,
79:   backreferences and look-around assertions are not supported. See
80:   [Syntax](https://github.com/google/re2/wiki/Syntax) for a description of what
81:   RE2 supports.
82: - Compiling a regular expression is likely to be slower, and thus more can be
83:   gained by explicitly compiling the regular expression before matching with it.
84: 
85: [](){: #float_matching }
86: 
87: ### 0\.0 and -0.0 will no longer be exactly equal
88: 
89: Currently, the floating point numbers `0.0` and `-0.0` have distinct internal
90: representations. That can be seen if they are converted to binaries:
91: 
92: ```erlang
93: 1> <<0.0/float>>.
94: <<0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0>>
95: 2> <<-0.0/float>>.
96: <<128,0,0,0,0,0,0,0>>
97: ```
98: 
99: However, when they are matched against each other or compared using the `=:=`
100: operator, they are considered to be equal. Thus, `0.0 =:= -0.0` currently
101: returns `true`.
102: 
103: In Erlang/OTP 27, `0.0 =:= -0.0` will return `false`, and matching `0.0` against
104: `-0.0` will fail. When used as map keys, `0.0` and `-0.0` will be considered to
105: be distinct.
106: 
107: The `==` operator will continue to return `true` for `0.0 == -0.0`.
108: 
109: To help to find code that might need to be revised, in OTP 27 there will be a
110: new compiler warning when matching against `0.0` or comparing to that value
111: using the `=:=` operator. The warning can be suppressed by matching against
112: `+0.0` instead of `0.0`.
113: 
114: We plan to introduce the same warning in OTP 26.1, but by default it will be
115: disabled.
116: 
117: [](){: #singleton_typevars }
118: 
119: ### Singleton type variables will become a compile-time error
120: 
121: Before Erlang/OTP 26, the compiler would silenty accept the following spec:
122: 
123: ```erlang
124: -spec f(Opts) -> term() when
125:     Opts :: {ok, Unknown} | {error, Unknown}.
126: f(_) -> error.
127: ```
128: 
129: In OTP 26, the compiler emits a warning pointing out that the type variable
130: `Unknown` is unbound:
131: 
132: ```erlang
133: t.erl:6:18: Warning: type variable 'Unknown' is only used once (is unbound)
134: %    6|     Opts :: {ok, Unknown} | {error, Unknown}.
135: %     |                  ^
136: ```
137: 
138: In OTP 27, that warning will become an error.
139: 
140: [](){: #escripts_will_be_compiled }
141: 
142: ### Escripts will be compiled by default
143: 
144: Escripts will be compiled by default instead of interpreted. That means that the
145: `compiler` application must be available.
146: 
147: The old behavior of interpreting escripts can be restored by adding the
148: following line to the script file:
149: 
150: ```erlang
151: -mode(interpret).
152: ```
153: 
154: In OTP 28, support for interpreting an escript will be removed.
155: 
156: ### \-code_path_choice will default to strict
157: 
158: This command line option controls if paths given in the command line, boot
159: scripts, and the code server should be interpreted as is strict or relaxed.
160: 
161: OTP 26 and earlier defaults to `relaxed`, which means `-pa myapp/ebin` would
162: attempt to load `-pa myapp/ebin` and `-pa myapp/myapp/ebin`. The option will
163: default to strict in OTP 27.
164: 
165: ### Archive fallbacks will be removed
166: 
167: OTP 26 and earlier allows an application to have part of its directories as
168: regular folders and others as archives. This functionality was previously used
169: by reltool but it is no longer the case from OTP 26. Support for archive
170: fallbacks will be removed from the code server in OTP 27.
171: 
172: [](){: #triple_quoted_strings }
173: 
174: ### Triple-Quoted Strings
175: 
176: Before Erlang/OTP 27 a sequence of 3 or more double-quote characters was grouped
177: in pairs each meaning the empty string and if there was an odd number the last
178: character was the start of a string. The empty strings were then concatenated
179: and effectively disappeared.
180: 
181: In Erlang/OTP 27; 3 or more double-quote characters are interpreted as the start
182: of a "Triple-Quoted String". See [EEP 64](https://www.erlang.org/eeps/eep-0064).
183: 
184: Here follows some examples of code that would change meaning. Note that all
185: these examples before Erlang/OTP 27.0 was strange since there was no sensible
186: reason to write like that.
187: 
188: ```erlang
189: """String Content"""
190: %% Was interpreted as
191: "" "String Content" ""
192: %% Which becomes
193: "String Content"
194: %%
195: %% In OTP 27 it is instead a syntax error since no text is allowed
196: %% on the line after an opening triple-quote
197: ```
198: 
199: ```text
200: """
201: String Content
202: """
203: %% Was interpreted as
204: "" "
205: String Content
206: " ""
207: %% Which becomes
208: "
209: String Content
210: "
211: %%
212: %% In OTP 27 it is instead interpreted as a
213: %% Triple-Quoted String equivalent to
214: "String Content"
215: ```
216: 
217: ```erlang
218: """"
219: ++ foo() ++
220: """"
221: %% Became
222: "" ++ foo() ++ ""
223: %%
224: %% In OTP 27 it is instead interpreted as a
225: %% Triple-Quoted String (triple-or-more) equivalent to
226: "++ foo() ++"
227: ```
228: 
229: From Erlang/OTP 26.1 up to 27.0 the compiler issues a warning for a sequence of
230: 3 or more double-quote characters since that is almost certainly a mistake or
231: something like a result of bad automatic code generation. If a users gets that
232: warning, the code should be corrected for example by inserting appropriate
233: spaces between the empty strings, or removing the redundant ones alltogether,
234: which will have the same meaning before and after Erlang/OTP 27.
235: 
236: ## OTP 28
237: 
238: [](){: #fun_creator_pid }
239: 
240: ### Fun creator pid will be removed
241: 
242: As of OTP 28, the function `erlang:fun_info/1` will not include the `{pid,_}`
243: element and the function `erlang:fun_info/2` will no longer accept `pid` as the
244: second argument.
245: 
246: [](){: #escript_interpret_mode_removed }
247: 
248: ### Support for interpreting escripts will be removed
249: 
250: Escripts will be compiled, and it will no longer be possible to force an escript
251: to be interpreted by using the directive `-mode(interpret)`.
252: 
253: ## OTP 29
254: 
255: ### It will no longer be possible to disable feature maybe_expr
256: 
257: As of OTP 29, the `maybe_expr` feature will become permanent and no longer
258: possible to disable. All uses of `maybe` as an atom will need to be quoted.
259: 
260: It is recommend to quote all uses of the atom `maybe` as soon as possible. The
261: compiler option `warn_keywords` can be used to emit warnings about all
262: occurrences of `maybe` without quotes.
263: 
264: ### cprof and eprof will be replaced by tprof
265: 
266: As of OTP 29, the `cprof` and `eprof` will be removed in favor of `m:tprof`
267: added in OTP 27.

251:     [{doc, "Tests pattern enable/disable correctness"}].
252: 
253: patterns(Config) when is_list(Config) ->
254:     {ok, _Srv} = tprof:start_link(#{type => call_memory}),
255:     %% test errors
256:     ?assertEqual({error, {not_traced, pg, get_members, '_'}}, tprof:clear_pattern(pg, get_members, '_')),
257:     ?assertEqual({error, {trace_pattern, ?MODULE, seq, 2}}, tprof:set_pattern(?MODULE, seq, 2)),
258:     %% successful patterns
259:     1 = tprof:set_pattern(?MODULE, seq, 1),
260:     3 = tprof:set_pattern(?MODULE, pattern_fun, '_'),
261:     1 = tprof:clear_pattern(?MODULE, pattern_fun, 2),
262:     Expected = [{pattern_fun, 1}, {pattern_fun, 3}, {seq, 1}],
263:     ?assertEqual(#{?MODULE => Expected}, tprof:get_trace_map()),
264:     %% verify tracing flags
265:     verify_trace([{?MODULE, F, A} || {F, A} <- Expected], [{?MODULE, pattern_fun, 2}]),
266:     %% trace the entire lists module, and then exclude pattern_fun/1,2,3 and seq/1
267:     _ = tprof:set_pattern(?MODULE, '_', '_'),
268:     3 = tprof:clear_pattern(?MODULE, pattern_fun, '_'),
269:     1 = tprof:clear_pattern(?MODULE, seq, 1),
270:     Cleared = [{pattern_fun, 1}, {pattern_fun, 2}, {pattern_fun, 3}, {seq, 1}],
271:     Traced = ?MODULE:module_info(functions) -- Cleared,
272:     verify_trace([{?MODULE, F, A} || {F, A} <- Traced], [{?MODULE, F, A} || {F, A} <- Cleared]),
273:     %% clear all, which clears lists too
274:     _ = tprof:clear_pattern('_', '_', '_'),
275:     verify_trace([], [{?MODULE, F, A} || {F, A} <- Traced ++ Cleared]),

297:     ?assertEqual({1, ['$sure_not_exist']}, tprof:enable_trace([Pid, '$sure_not_exist'])),

301: server() ->
302:     [{doc, "Tests for gen_server-based API"}].
303: 
304: server(Config) when is_list(Config) ->
305:     %% start an extra pg scope - we'll trace it during profiling
306:     {ok, Scope} = pg:start_link(?FUNCTION_NAME),
307:     %% simulate existing process
308:     Pid = spawn_link(fun spawn_loop/0),
309:     %% start the profiler
310:     {ok, Srv} = tprof:start_link(#{type => call_memory}),
311:     %% test ad-hoc profile clash
312:     ?assertException(error, {already_started, Srv}, tprof:profile(fun spawn_loop/0)),
313:     %% test live trace
314:     1 = tprof:set_pattern(?MODULE, dispatch, '_'),
315:     _ = tprof:set_pattern(pg, '_', '_'),
316:     %% watch for pg traces and for our process
317:     2 = tprof:enable_trace([Pid, ?FUNCTION_NAME]),
318:     %% run the traced operation
319:     _ = gen_server:call(Pid, {apply, pg, join, [?FUNCTION_NAME, group, Pid]}),
320:     %% collect profile (can save it to a file for later analysis)
321:     {call_memory, FirstProfile} = tprof:collect(),
322:     %% must not be empty, and must contain 3-words dispatch from this module,
323:     %%  and at least something from pg in two processes
324:     ?assertNotEqual([], FirstProfile),
325:     ?assertEqual({?MODULE, dispatch, 2, [{Pid, 1, 3}]}, lists:keyfind(?MODULE, 1, FirstProfile)),
326:     ?assertMatch({pg, handle_call, 3, [{Scope, _, _}]}, lists:keyfind(handle_call, 2, FirstProfile)),
327:     ?assertMatch({pg, join, 3, [{Pid, _, _}]}, lists:keyfind(join, 2, FirstProfile)),
328:     %% pause tracing
329:     ok = tprof:pause(),
330:     %% ensure paused by running more code but keeping the trace
331:     %% ensure collection still returns the previous result
332:     _ = gen_server:call(Pid, {apply, pg, join, [?FUNCTION_NAME, group, Pid]}),
333:     {call_memory, FirstProfile} = tprof:collect(),
334:     %% continue, ensure new results are collected
335:     ok = tprof:continue(),
336:     _ = gen_server:call(Pid, {apply, pg, leave, [?FUNCTION_NAME, group, [Pid, Pid]]}),
337:     ?assertNotEqual({call_memory, FirstProfile}, tprof:collect()),
338:     %% restart all counters from zero and ensure that we again collect the original data
339:     ok = tprof:restart(),
340:     _ = gen_server:call(Pid, {apply, pg, join, [?FUNCTION_NAME, group, Pid]}),
341:     {call_memory, FirstProfile} = tprof:collect(),
342:

# Profiling

## Never Guess About Performance Bottlenecks

Even experienced software developers often guess wrong about where the
performance bottlenecks are in their programs. Therefore, profile your program
to see where the performance bottlenecks are and concentrate on optimizing them.

Erlang/OTP contains several tools to help find bottlenecks:

- `m:tprof` is a tracing profiler that can measure call count, call time, or
  heap allocations per function call.
- `m:fprof` provides the most detailed information about where the program time
  is spent, but it significantly slows down the program it profiles.
- `m:dbg` is the generic Erlang tracing frontend. By using the `timestamp` or
  `cpu_timestamp` options it can be used to time how long function calls in a
  live system take.
- `m:lcnt` is used to find contention points in the Erlang Run-Time System's
  internal locking mechanisms. It is useful when looking for bottlenecks in
  interaction between processes, ports, ETS tables, and other entities that can be
  run in parallel.

The tools are further described in [Tools](profiling.md#profiling_tools).

There are also several open source tools outside of Erlang/OTP that can be used
to help profiling. Some of them are:

- [erlgrind](https://github.com/isacssouza/erlgrind) can be used to visualize
  fprof data in kcachegrind.
- [eflame](https://github.com/proger/eflame) is an alternative to fprof that
  displays the profiling output as a flamegraph.
- [recon](https://ferd.github.io/recon/index.html) is a collection of Erlang
  profiling and debugging tools. This tool comes with an accompanying E-book
  called [Erlang in Anger](https://www.erlang-in-anger.com/).
- [perf](https://perf.wiki.kernel.org/index.php/Main_Page) is a sampling
  profiler for Linux that provides functionality similar to `fprof` but with
  much lower overhead. Profiling Erlang code is possible when the emulator has
  been started with the `+JPperf true` emulator flag, and is only available when
  the JIT is enabled.

  For more details about how to run `perf` see the
  [perf support](`e:erts:beamasm.md#linux-perf-support`) section in the BeamAsm
  internal documentation.

## Memory profiling

```text
eheap_alloc: Cannot allocate 1234567890 bytes of memory (of type "heap").
```

The above slogan is one of the more common reasons for Erlang to terminate. For
unknown reasons the Erlang Run-Time System failed to allocate memory to use.
When this happens a crash dump is generated that contains information about the
state of the system as it ran out of memory. Use
[`crashdump_viewer`](`e:observer:cdv_cmd.md`) to get a view of the memory being
used. Look for processes with large heaps or many messages, large ETS tables,
and so on.

## Tools

[](){: #profiling_tools }

### fprof

`fprof` measures the execution time for each function, both own time, that is,
how much time a function has used for its own execution, and accumulated time,
that is, including called functions. The values are displayed per process. You
also get to know how many times each function has been called.

`fprof` is based on trace to file to minimize runtime performance impact. Using
`fprof` is just a matter of calling a few library functions, see the `m:fprof`
manual page in Tools.

### eprof

`eprof` is based on the Erlang `trace_info` BIFs. `eprof` shows how much time
has been used by each process, and in which function calls this time has been
spent. Time is shown as a percentage of total time and absolute time. For more
information, see the `m:eprof` manual page in Tools.

### cprof

`cprof` is something in between `fprof` and `cover` regarding features. It
counts how many times each function is called when the program is run, on a per
module basis. `cprof` has a low performance degradation effect (compared with
`fprof`) and does not need to recompile any modules to profile (compared with
`cover`). For more information, see the `m:cprof` manual page in Tools.

### Tool Summary

|                                       | fprof                      | eprof                               | cprof                |
| ------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| **Results**                           | Per process to screen/file | Per process/function to screen/file | Per module to caller |
| **Size of Result**                    | Large                      | Medium                              | Small                |
| **Effects on Program Execution Time** | Significant slowdown       | Small slowdown                      | Small slowdown       |
| **Records Number of Calls**           | Yes                        | Yes                                 | Yes                  |
| **Records Execution Time**            | Total and own              | Only total                          | No                   |
| **Records Called by**                 | Yes                        | No                                  | No                   |
| **Records Garbage Collection**        | Yes                        | No                                  | No                   |

_Table: Tool Summary_

### dbg

`dbg` is a generic Erlang trace tool. By using the `timestamp` or
`cpu_timestamp` options it can be used as a precision instrument to profile how
long a function call takes for a specific process. This can be very useful
when trying to understand where time is spent in a heavily loaded system as it
is possible to limit the scope of what is profiled to be very small. For more
information, see the `m:dbg` manual page in Runtime Tools.

### lcnt

`lcnt` is used to profile interactions between entities that run in parallel.
For example if you have a process that all other processes in the system need
to interact with (maybe it has some global configuration), then `lcnt` can be
used to figure out if the interaction with that process is a problem.

In the Erlang Run-Time System entities are only run in parallel when there are
multiple schedulers. Therefore `lcnt` will show more contention points (and thus
be more useful) on systems using many schedulers on many cores.

For more information, see the `m:lcnt` manual page in Tools.

%% analyze the result of one test run, or many (in case of looped test)
analyze_test_result(ok, _) ->
    ?EXIT_STATUS_TEST_SUCCESSFUL;
analyze_test_result({error,_Reason}, _) ->
    ?EXIT_STATUS_TEST_RUN_FAILED;
analyze_test_result({_Ok,Failed,{_UserSkipped,AutoSkipped}}, Args) ->
    if Failed > 0 ->
	    ?EXIT_STATUS_TEST_CASE_FAILED;
       true ->
	    case AutoSkipped of
		0 ->
		    ?EXIT_STATUS_TEST_SUCCESSFUL;
		_ ->
		    case get_start_opt(exit_status,
				       fun([ExitOpt]) -> ExitOpt end,
				       Args) of
			undefined ->
			    ?EXIT_STATUS_TEST_CASE_FAILED;
			"ignore_config" ->
		    	    ?EXIT_STATUS_TEST_SUCCESSFUL
		    end
	    end
    end;
analyze_test_result([Result|Rs], Args) ->
    case analyze_test_result(Result, Args) of
	?EXIT_STATUS_TEST_SUCCESSFUL ->
	    analyze_test_result(Rs, Args);
	Other ->
	    Other
    end;
analyze_test_result([], _) ->
    ?EXIT_STATUS_TEST_SUCCESSFUL;
analyze_test_result(interactive_mode, _) ->
    interactive_mode;

253: ## Example: Extracting Data From XML Content
254: 
255: In this example consider the situation where you want to examine a particular
256: data in the XML file. For instance, you want to check for how long each
257: motorcycle have been recorded.
258: 
259: Take a look at the DTD and observe that the structure of an XML document that is
260: conformant to this DTD must have one motorcycles element (the root element). The
261: motorcycles element must have at least one bike element. After each bike element
262: it may be a date element. The content of the date element is #PCDATA (Parsed
263: Character DATA), i.e. raw text. Observe that if #PCDATA must have a `"<"` or a
264: `"&"` character it must be written as `"<"` and `"&"` respectively. Also
265: other character entities exists similar to the ones in HTML and SGML.
266: 
267: If you successfully parse the XML file with the validation on as in:
268: `xmerl_scan:file('motorcycles.xml',[{validation,true}])` you know that the XML
269: document is valid and has the structure according to the DTD.
270: 
271: Thus, knowing the allowed structure it is easy to write a program that traverses
272: the data structure and picks the information in the xmlElements records with
273: name date.
274: 
275: Observe that white space: each space, tab or line feed, between mark-up results
276: in an xmlText record.
277: 
278: ## Example: Create XML Out Of Arbitrary Data
279: 
280: For this task there are more than one way to go. The "brute force" method is to
281: create the records you need and feed your data in the content and attribute
282: fields of the appropriate element.
283: 
284: There is support for this in xmerl by the "simple-form" format. You can put your
285: data in a simple-form data structure and feed it into
286: `xmerl:export_simple(Content,Callback,RootAttributes)`. Content may be a mixture
287: of simple-form and xmerl records as xmlElement and xmlText.
288: 
289: The Types are:
290: 
291: - Content = \[Element]
292: - Callback = atom()
293: - RootAttributes = \[Attributes]
294: 
295: Element is any of:
296: 
297: - \{Tag, Attributes, Content\}
298: - \{Tag, Content\}
299: - Tag
300: - IOString
301: - \#xmlText\{\}
302: - \#xmlElement\{\}
303: - \#xmlPI\{\}
304: - \#xmlComment\{\}
305: - \#xmlDecl\{\}
306: 
307: The simple-form structure is any of `{Tag, Attributes, Content}`,
308: `{Tag, Content}` or `Tag` where:
309: 
310: - Tag = atom()
311: - Attributes = \[\{Name, Value\}| #xmlAttribute\{\}]
312: - Name = atom()
313: - Value = IOString | atom() | integer()
314: 
315: See also reference manual for [xmerl](`xmerl:export_simple/3`)
316: 
317: If you want to add the information about a black Harley Davidsson 1200 cc
318: Sportster motorcycle from 2003 that is in shape as new in the motorcycles.xml
319: document you can put the data in a simple-form data structure like:
320: 
321: ```erlang
322: Data =
323:   {bike,
324:      [{year,"2003"},{color,"black"},{condition,"new"}],
325:      [{name,
326:          [{manufacturer,["Harley Davidsson"]},
327:           {brandName,["XL1200C"]},
328:           {additionalName,["Sportster"]}]},
329:       {engine,
330:          ["V-engine, 2-cylinders, 1200 cc"]},
331:       {kind,["custom"]},
332:       {drive,["belt"]}]}
333: ```
334: 
335: In order to append this data to the end of the motorcycles.xml document you have
336: to parse the file and add Data to the end of the root element content.
337: 
338: ```erlang
339:     {RootEl,Misc}=xmerl_scan:file('motorcycles.xml'),
340:     #xmlElement{content=Content} = RootEl,
341:     NewContent=Content++lists:flatten([Data]),
342:     NewRootEl=RootEl#xmlElement{content=NewContent},
343: ```
344: 
345: Then you can run it through the export_simple/2 function:
346:

348:     {ok,IOF}=file:open('new_motorcycles.xml',[write]),
349:     Export=xmerl:export_simple([NewRootEl],xmerl_xml),
350:     io:format(IOF,"~s~n",[lists:flatten(Export)]),

## Problem

When `io_lib:get_until` is used with a `get_until` function that returns data at end-of-file (EOF), the result is incorrectly returned as a list (or in the wrong type) instead of a binary when the initial data was binary. This breaks binary-mode I/O operations that rely on `get_until` for tokenized input.

Specifically, the current implementation in `io_lib:get_until/4` uses the type of the *current* data chunk to decide whether to convert the result to a binary. When EOF is reached, the data chunk is `eof` (not a binary), so the conversion logic is skipped, and the result is returned as a list even though the caller expected binary output.

## Required Changes

Fix `io_lib:get_until/4` so that when the *initial* data passed to the function was binary (indicating binary mode), the final result is always converted to binary, including when the result is returned at EOF. Track the initial data type across continuation states so it can be used at EOF.

Additionally, improve error handling in `file_io_server` for invalid Unicode errors related to `io_lib:get_until` to ensure the error reporting is correct regardless of the continuation state.

Finally, add tests to verify that `get_until` returns binaries (or lists) correctly in both binary and list modes, including at EOF.

Also check `lib/kernel/src/Makefile` and `lib/stdlib/src/Makefile` for how the modules are compiled.

- Modify the `get_until` clauses in `lib/stdlib/src/io_lib.erl` so the continuation state carries a flag (e.g., a boolean) indicating whether the initial data was binary. 20: # List Comprehensions
21: 
22: ## Simple Examples
23: 
24: This section starts with a simple example, showing a generator and a filter:
25: 
26: ```text
27: > [X || X <- [1,2,a,3,4,b,5,6], X > 3].
28: [a,4,b,5,6]
29: ```
30: 
31: This is read as follows: The list of X such that X is taken from the list
32: `[1,2,a,...]` and X is greater than 3.
33: 
34: The notation `X <- [1,2,a,...]` is a generator and the expression `X > 3` is a
35: filter.
36: 
37: An additional filter, [`is_integer(X)`](`is_integer/1`), can be added to
38: restrict the result to integers:
39: 
40: ```erlang
41: > [X || X <- [1,2,a,3,4,b,5,6], is_integer(X), X > 3].
42: [4,5,6]
43: ```
44: 
45: Generators can be combined. For example, the Cartesian product of two lists can
46: be written as follows:
47: 
48: ```erlang
49: > [{X, Y} || X <- [1,2,3], Y <- [a,b]].
50: [{1,a},{1,b},{2,a},{2,b},{3,a},{3,b}]
51: ```
52: 
53: ## Quick Sort
54: 
55: The well-known quick sort routine can be written as follows:
56: 
57: ```erlang
58: sort([]) -> [];
59: sort([_] = L) -> L;
60: sort([Pivot|T]) ->
61:     sort([ X || X <- T, X < Pivot]) ++
62:     [Pivot] ++
63:     sort([ X || X <- T, X >= Pivot]).
64: ```
65: 
66: The expression `[X || X <- T, X < Pivot]` is the list of all elements in `T`
67: that are less than `Pivot`.
68: 
69: `[X || X <- T, X >= Pivot]` is the list of all elements in `T` that are greater
70: than or equal to `Pivot`.
71: 
72: With the algorithm above, a list is sorted as follows:
73: 
74: - A list with zero or one element is trivially sorted.
75: - For lists with more than one element:
76:   1. The first element in the list is isolated as the pivot element.
77:   1. The remaining list is partitioned into two sublists, such that:
78:   - The first sublist contains all elements that are smaller than the pivot
79:     element.
80:   - The second sublist contains all elements that are greater than or equal to
81:     the pivot element.
82:   1. The sublists are recursively sorted by the same algorithm and the results
83:      are combined, resulting in a list consisting of:
84:   - All elements from the first sublist, that is all elements smaller than the
85:     pivot element, in sorted order.
86:   - The pivot element.
87:   - All elements from the second sublist, that is all elements greater than or
88:     equal to the pivot element, in sorted order.
89: 
90: > #### Note {: .info }
91: >
92: > While the sorting algorithm as shown above serves as a nice example to
93: > illustrate list comprehensions with filters, for real world use cases the
94: > `m:lists` module contains sorting functions that are implemented in a more
95: > efficient way.
96: 
97: ## Permutations
98: 
99: The following example generates all permutations of the elements in a list:
100: 
101: ```erlang
102: perms([]) -> [[]];
103: perms(L)  -> [[H|T] || H <- L, T <- perms(L--[H])].
104: ```
105: 
106: This takes `H` from `L` in all possible ways. The result is the set of all lists
107: `[H|T]`, where `T` is the set of all possible permutations of `L`, with `H`
108: removed:
109: 
110: ```text
111: > perms([b,u,g]).
112: [[b,u,g],[b,g,u],[u,b,g],[u,g,b],[g,b,u],[g,u,b]]
113: ```
114: 
115: ## Pythagorean Triplets
116: 
117: Pythagorean triplets are sets of integers `{A,B,C}` such that
118: `A**2 + B**2 = C**2`.
119: 
120: The function `pyth(N)` generates a list of all integers `{A,B,C}` such that
121: `A**2 + B**2 = C**2` and where the sum of the sides is equal to, or less than,
122: `N`:
123: 
124: ```erlang
125: pyth(N) ->
126:     [ {A,B,C} ||
127:         A <- lists:seq(1,N),
128:         B <- lists:seq(1,N),
129:         C <- lists:seq(1,N),
130:         A+B+C =< N,
131:         A*A+B*B == C*C
132:     ].
133: ```
134: 
135: ```erlang
136: > pyth(3).
137: [].
138: > pyth(11).
139: [].
140: > pyth(12).
141: [{3,4,5},{4,3,5}]
142: > pyth(50).
143: [{3,4,5},
144:  {4,3,5},
145:  {5,12,13},
146:  {6,8,10},
147:  {8,6,10},
148:  {8,15,17},
149:  {9,12,15},
150:  {12,5,13},
151:  {12,9,15},
152:  {12,16,20},
153:  {15,8,17},
154:  {16,12,20}]
155: ```
156: 
157: The following code reduces the search space and is more efficient:
158: 
159: ```erlang
160: pyth1(N) ->
161:    [{A,B,C} ||
162:        A <- lists:seq(1,N-2),
163:        B <- lists:seq(A+1,N-1),
164:        C <- lists:seq(B+1,N),
165:        A+B+C =< N,
166:        A*A+B*B == C*C ].
167: ```
168: 
169: ## Simplifications With List Comprehensions
170: 
171: As an example, list comprehensions can be used to simplify some of the functions
172: in `lists.erl`:
173: 
174: ```erlang
175: append(L)   ->  [X || L1 <- L, X <- L1].
176: map(Fun, L) -> [Fun(X) || X <- L].
177: filter(Pred, L) -> [X || X <- L, Pred(X)].
178: ```
179: 
180: ## Variable Bindings in List Comprehensions
181: 
182: The scope rules for variables that occur in list comprehensions are as follows:
183: 
184: - All variables that occur in a generator pattern are assumed to be "fresh"
185:   variables.
186: - Any variables that are defined before the list comprehension, and that are
187:   used in filters, have the values they had before the list comprehension.
188: - Variables cannot be exported from a list comprehension.
189: 
190: As an example of these rules, suppose you want to write the function `select`,
191: which selects certain elements from a list of tuples. Suppose you write
192: `select(X, L) -> [Y || {X, Y} <- L].` with the intention of extracting all
193: tuples from `L`, where the first item is `X`.
194: 
195: Compiling this gives the following diagnostic:
196: 
197: ```text
198: ./FileName.erl:Line: Warning: variable 'X' shadowed in generate
199: ```
200: 
201: This diagnostic warns that the variable `X` in the pattern is not the same as
202: the variable `X` that occurs in the function head.
203: 
204: Evaluating `select` gives the following result:
205: 
206: ```erlang
207: > select(b,[{a,1},{b,2},{c,3},{b,7}]).
208: [1,2,3,7]
209: ```
210: 
211: This is not the wanted result. To achieve the desired effect, `select` must be
212: written as follows:
213: 
214: ```erlang
215: select(X, L) ->  [Y || {X1, Y} <- L, X == X1].
216: ```
217: 
218: The generator now contains unbound variables and the test has been moved into
219: the filter.
220: 
221: This now works as expected:
222: 
223: ```erlang
224: > select(b,[{a,1},{b,2},{c,3},{b,7}]).
225: [2,7]
226: ```
227: 
228: Also note that a variable in a generator pattern will shadow a variable with the
229: same name bound in a previous generator pattern. For example:
230: 
231: ```erlang
232: > [{X,Y} || X <- [1,2,3], X=Y <- [a,b,c]].
233: [{a,a},{b,b},{c,c},{a,a},{b,b},{c,c},{a,a},{b,b},{c,c}]
234: ```
235: 
236: A consequence of the rules for importing variables into a list comprehensions is
237: that certain pattern matching operations must be moved into the filters and
238: cannot be written directly in the generators.
239: 
240: To illustrate this, do _not_ write as follows:
241: 
242: ```text
243: f(...) ->
244:     Y = ...
245:     [ Expression || PatternInvolving Y  <- Expr, ...]
246:     ...
247: ```
248: 
249: Instead, write as follows:
250: 
251: ```text
252: f(...) ->
253:     Y = ...
254:     [ Expression || PatternInvolving Y1  <- Expr, Y == Y1, ...]
255:     ...
256: ```

50: support per-process profiling. For this reason, all of the examples below use
51: `call_memory`, which measures heap allocation, and provide a more complex
52: feature set to demonstrate.

54: Heap allocations happen for all Erlang terms that do not fit a single machine
55: word. For example, a function returning tuple of 2 elements needs to allocate
56: this tuple on the process heap. Actual consumption is more than 2 machine words,

%% @doc Collects memory tracing data (usable for inspect()) for
%%      all traced functions.
-spec collect(trace_map(), trace_type()) -> {trace_type(), [trace_info()]}.
collect(Pattern, Type) ->
    {Type,
        maps:fold(fun(K, V, Acc) -> collect_trace(K, V, Acc, Type) end, [],
            Pattern)
        ++ collect_on_load(Pattern, Type)}.

%% Collects tracing data for modules that got loaded after profiling was
%%  started. Those modules are not present in the trace map, but their
%%  functions are traced via the on-load trace pattern.
collect_on_load(Pattern, Type) ->
    case erlang:trace_info(on_load, Type) of
        {_, true} ->
            lists:foldl(
                fun ({Mod, _}, Acc) ->
                    case is_map_key(Mod, Pattern) of
                        true ->
                            Acc;
                        false ->
                            collect_new_trace(Mod, functions(Mod), Acc, Type)
                    end
                end, [], code:all_loaded());
        {_, false} ->
            []
    end.

functions(Module) ->
    try Module:module_info(functions)
    catch error:undef -> []
    end.

%% Collect tracing info for a module that may not have been traced, quietly
%%  skipping functions without an active trace.
collect_new_trace(_Mod, [], Acc, _Type) ->
    Acc;
collect_new_trace(Mod, [{Fun, Arity} | Rest], Acc, Type) ->
    case combine_trace(erlang:trace_info({Mod, Fun, Arity}, Type)) of
        skip ->
            collect_new_trace(Mod, Rest, Acc, Type);
        fail ->
            collect_new_trace(Mod, Rest, Acc, Type);
        Tr ->
            collect_new_trace(Mod, Rest, [{Mod, Fun, Arity, Tr} | Acc], Type)
    end.

-export([main/0, test_spawn/0]).

main() ->
    println("===C===", {call_memory, [
        {erlang, spawn_monitor, 1, [{c:pid(0, 176, 0), 1, 2}]},
        {erlang, spawn_opt, 4, [{c:pid(0, 176, 0), 1, 6}]},
        {test, test_spawn, 0, [{c:pid(0, 176, 0), 1, 14}]},
        {erlang, apply, 2, [{c:pid(0, 177, 0), 1, 7}]},
        {lists, seq_loop, 3, [{c:pid(0, 177, 0), 9, 64}]}]}, 0),
    println("===D===", {call_memory, [
        {lists, seq_loop, 3, [{c:pid(0, 177, 0), 9, 64}]},
        {test, test_spawn, 0, [{c:pid(0, 176, 0), 1, 14}]},
        {erlang, apply, 2, [{c:pid(0, 177, 0), 1, 7}]},
        {erlang, spawn_opt, 4, [{c:pid(0, 176, 0), 1, 6}]},
        {erlang, spawn_monitor, 1, [{c:pid(0, 176, 0), 1, 2}]}]}, 1),
    println("===E===", {call_memory, [
        {erlang, spawn_monitor, 1, [{c:pid(0, 183, 0), 1, 2}]},
        {erlang, spawn_opt, 4, [{c:pid(0, 183, 0), 1, 6}]},
        {test, test_spawn, 0, [{c:pid(0, 183, 0), 1, 14}]}]}, 0),
    halt().

println(Tag, Profile, Total) ->
    io:format("~s~n", [Tag]),
    Insp = case Total of
        0 -> tprof:inspect(Profile, process, percent);
        1 -> tprof:inspect(Profile, total, {measurement, descending})
    end,
    tprof:format(group_leader(), Insp).

test_spawn() ->
    {Pid, MRef} = spawn_monitor(fun () -> lists:seq(1, 32) end),
    receive
        {'DOWN', MRef, process, Pid, normal} ->
            done
    end.

77: ## Ad-hoc profiling
78: 
79: Basic profiling providing accumulated memory allocation data. You can choose to
80: print per-process statistics, total statistics, or omit printing and extract
81: machine-readable data that you can later sort/print:
82: 
83: ```text
84:       1> tprof:profile(lists, seq, [1, 16], #{type => call_memory}).
85: 
86:       ****** Process <0.179.0>  --  100.00% of total *** 
87:       FUNCTION          CALLS  WORDS  PER CALL  [     %]
88:       lists:seq_loop/3      5     32      6.40  [100.00]
89:                                   32            [ 100.0]
90:       ok
91: ```
92: 
93: By default tracing is enabled for all functions of all modules. When functions
94: are created in the interactive shell, parts of shell code are also traced. It is
95: however possible to limit the trace to specific functions or modules:
96: 
97: ```erlang
98:       1> tprof:profile(fun() -> lists:seq(1, 16) end, #{type => call_memory}).
99: 
100:       ****** Process <0.224.0>  --  100.00% of total *** 
101:       FUNCTION                   CALLS  WORDS  PER CALL  [    %]
102:       erl_eval:do_apply/7            1      3      3.00  [ 3.19]
103:       erl_eval:match_list/6          1      3      3.00  [ 3.19]

105:       erl_eval:add_bindings/2        1      5      5.00  [ 5.32]

107:       erl_eval:ret_expr/3            4     16      4.00  [17.02]

109:       lists:seq_loop/3               5     32      6.40  [34.04]
110:                                            94            [100.0]

115:       FUNCTION          CALLS  WORDS  PER CALL  [     %]
116:       lists:seq_loop/3      5     32      6.40  [100.00]

125:       -export([test_spawn/0]).

128:           receive

130:                   done
131:           end.
132: ```

134: Default format prints per-process statistics.
135: 
136: ```text
137:         2> tprof:profile(test, test_spawn, [], #{type => call_memory}).
138: 
139:         ****** Process <0.176.0>  --  23.66% of total *** 
140:         FUNCTION                CALLS  WORDS  PER CALL  [    %]
141:         erlang:spawn_monitor/1      1      2      2.00  [ 9.09]

149:         lists:seq_loop/3      9     64      7.11  [90.14]
